stories.title: Barings Provides $73M Loan on Needham Office Campus Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Barings said Monday it has provided a $72.6 million loan to a joint venture between Cross Ocean Partners and Lincoln Property Company to support the acquisition of 140 Kendrick St., a Class A office campus in Needham, MA. The partnership acquired the campus from BXP in December 2025 in a $132-million deal brokered by Newmark “We are pleased to support Cross Ocean Partners and Lincoln Property Company in financing 140 Kendrick St.,” said Jonathan Neff, managing director at Barings. “The property’s experienced sponsorship, strong fundamentals, and leasing momentum make it a compelling investment opportunity to deploy capital on behalf of our investors.” 140 Kendrick St. is a three-building, interconnected office campus totaling 409,197 square feet across 14.3 acres and located approximately 15 miles southwest of Downtown Boston. It offers direct access to Route 128 / Interstate 95 and is adjacent to the 600-acre Cutler Park Reservation. The post Barings Provides $73M Loan on Needham Office Campus Acquisition appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Barings finances $72.6M loan for Cross Ocean/Lincoln Property's $132M office acquisition in Needham, MA.
409K SF, 14.3-acre Class A campus 15 miles southwest of Boston with strong leasing momentum.
Office capital remains available for stabilized, leased assets; no multifamily relevance.
stories.summary: Barings provided a $72.6 million loan to support Cross Ocean Partners and Lincoln Property Company's December 2025 acquisition of 140 Kendrick St., a 409,197 SF Class A office campus in Needham, MA, purchased from Boston Properties for $132 million. The three-building campus offers direct Route 128/I-95 access and sits on 14.3 acres near Cutler Park Reservation. The lender cited strong fundamentals and leasing momentum as drivers of investment appeal.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Office capital availability and strong Boston-area office leasing signal broader commercial real estate confidence, but does not inform apartment supply, demand, or cost drivers in the region.

stories.title: Kidder Mathews Arranges Sale of Capitol Hill Apartment Building
stories.excerpt: Vitality on Howell, a five-story apartment building located at 1420 E. Howell Street in Seattle’s Capitol Hill neighborhood, has sold. Jerrid Anderson, Jack Shephard, Matt Laird, and Matt Johnston of Kidder Mathews’ Simon | Anderson Multifamily Team represented the seller, a private investor and developer. Constructed in 2016, Vitality on Howell consists of 57 small efficiency dwelling units, averaging 297 square feet. The smaller footprint units provide an alternative to traditional studio and one-bedroom apartments while offering residents the privacy and functionality of an individual dwelling. The property is in close proximity to major employers and employment centers, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Nordstrom, and Seattle’s First Hill medical corridor, home to Swedish, Virginia Mason, and Harborview. “With limited new multifamily supply in recent years, Capitol Hill continues to attract renters seeking convenient access to light rail, major employment centers, and a vibrant mix of neighborhood amenities,” said Anderson. bullets: Vitality on Howell, 57-unit efficiency building, sold in Seattle Capitol Hill submarket.
Built 2016, avg 297 SF units; proximity to Amazon, Google, Meta, and First Hill medical corridor.
Limited recent multifamily supply drives continued renter demand despite tight downtown Seattle market.
stories.summary: Vitality on Howell, a 57-unit, five-story apartment building completed in 2016 on Seattle's Capitol Hill, changed hands with Kidder Mathews' multifamily team representing the private seller. Units average 297 SF, marketed as micro-efficiencies bridging studio and one-bedroom segments. The property benefits from proximity to major tech employers (Amazon, Google, Meta) and Seattle's First Hill medical corridor.
stories.impact: Capitol Hill's limited new multifamily deliveries in recent years are driving persistent renter demand and supporting tight occupancy and pricing. This sale signals strong investor appetite for newer, smaller-unit product near major employment; developers should prioritize infill or redevelopment sites in Capitol Hill and similar supply-constrained Seattle submarkets to capture demand before further rent escalation prices out middle-income renters.

stories.title: Biotech Firm Nears 700K-SF Lease at Former Google Hub
stories.excerpt: Revolution Medicines Inc. is nearing an agreement to lease 700,000 square feet at Pacific Shores Center in Redwood City, a former Google hub on the city’s bayfront, the Silicon Valley Business Journal reported. The lease would more than double the biotech company’s existing Redwood City presence as it prepares for a commercial launch of daraxonrasib, a pancreatic cancer drug that could generate billions of dollars in annual sales. The lease would come during a period of transition for Pacific Shores, a 106-acre waterfront office campus at the end of Seaport Boulevard. The property became closely associated with Google after the tech giant bought much of the campus in 2014 and later used it as a major Peninsula hub. Google has not occupied the campus since July 2024 and recently sold it, reported the Business Journal. Revolution’s move would also occur amid a biotech downturn that has left much of the Bay Area’s new lab space struggling to find tenants. The post Biotech Firm Nears 700K-SF Lease at Former Google Hub appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Revolution Medicines negotiating 700K SF lease at Pacific Shores, Redwood City—70% of Google's former hub.
Biotech expansion driven by commercial launch of pancreatic cancer drug; Google vacated July 2024.
Biotech sector downturn limiting lab-space absorption; Revolution's deal counters broader Bay Area weakness.
stories.summary: Revolution Medicines is nearing a 700,000 SF lease at Pacific Shores Center in Redwood City, a 106-acre former Google campus from which Google departed in July 2024 after the tech giant recently sold the property. The move would double Revolution's existing Redwood City footprint as it prepares for commercial launch of daraxonrasib, a pancreatic cancer treatment with potential multi-billion-dollar annual sales. The lease represents a significant absorption event amid a struggling Bay Area biotech lab-space market.
stories.impact: Google's exit from Pacific Shores and the biotech sector's broader downturn suggest longer-term softening in Redwood City office/lab demand; however, Revolution's lease is a bright spot for life-sciences real estate. For multifamily developers in the Peninsula and South Bay, this signals that biotech job growth is concentrated in select high-value facilities and commercial launches, not broad-based expansion. Monitor life-sciences clusters for stable employment anchors, but do not assume sector-wide growth will drive regional apartment demand as it once did.

stories.title: Bonaventure Acquires Ownership Interest in Chevy Chase MF Development
stories.excerpt: Bonaventure has acquired an ownership interest in Crescent at Chevy Chase, a 111-home community at 3929 Landmark Court in Chevy Chase, Maryland, from Landmark Realty, Inc., the Chevy Chase-based firm that developed the property. Bonaventure’s investment was made through Bonaventure Multifamily Income Trust, a non-traded real estate investment trust sponsored by Bonaventure. Bonaventure has assumed asset management of the community, and Willow Bridge Property Company has been engaged as the property manager. Landmark Realty, which designed, developed and has operated Crescent since its delivery, remains a partner in the ownership group. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Jorge Rosa, Marshall Scallan, TJ Liberto, Mac Hollensteiner and Jack Hillman of Cushman & Wakefield advised Landmark Realty. Cushman & Wakefield and Greystone arranged financing for the transaction. Delivered in 2024, Crescent at Chevy Chase comprises 111 apartment homes, averaging 846 square feet across studio, one-bedroom, two-bedroom and three-bedroom floor plans. bullets: Bonaventure acquires ownership stake in Crescent at Chevy Chase, 111-unit 2024-delivered building.
Landmark Realty retains partnership; Bonaventure REIT assumes asset management; Willow Bridge manages operations.
Recently stabilized product attracting institutional capital and professional management; modest transaction size, no disclosed pricing.
stories.summary: Bonaventure, through its non-traded multifamily REIT, acquired an ownership interest in Crescent at Chevy Chase, a 111-unit community delivered in 2024 in suburban Maryland. Original developer Landmark Realty remains a partner. Bonaventure assumed asset management while Willow Bridge was engaged as property manager. Unit mix includes studios through three-bedrooms averaging 846 SF.
stories.impact: Minimal direct market signal. The transaction reflects institutional REIT appetite for newly stabilized, market-rate suburban multifamily product in the Washington DC metro, but no material supply, demand, or cost implications for the development pipeline. Chevy Chase's build-out is mature; focus instead on growth submarkets in Fairfax County and outer DC rings.

stories.title: REBNY: Construction Filings Drop Sharply in Q2
stories.excerpt: New York City developers filed plans for approximately 9.2 million square feet of new construction across 387 new building filings in the second quarter of 2026, representing declines of 56% and 33%, respectively, from Q1, according to the Real Esytate Board iof New York (REBNY). Of those 387 filings, 172 were for proposed multiple-dwelling buildings totaling just 8,064 units, down 52% from Q1, REBNY said in its New Building Construction Pipeline Report. That is less than half of the 17,500 units per quarter the city now says are needed to build 700,000 new homes over the next decade and address the housing shortage. The decline in filings from Q1 to Q2 comes as New York City’s development pipeline shifts away from projects vested under 421-a and toward projects that must rely on 485-x or other funding programs. Q2 filings show a notable concentration of multifamily projects below the 100-unit threshold, while filings for projects with 100 units or more fell from 25 in Q1 to just 9 in Q2. “The decline in proposed construction this quarter is a warning sign that New York has not yet created the conditions and incentives needed to maintain the momentum of consistently delivering new homes at the scale required to address the city’s housing supply crisis,” said Basha Gerhards, REBNY EVP of public policy. The post REBNY: Construction Filings Drop Sharply in Q2 appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NYC Q2 2026 construction filings plunge 56% in SF (9.2M), 33% in count (387 buildings).
Multifamily filings collapse 52% to 8,064 units (Q1 was 17,500); only 9 projects 100+ units filed.
Pipeline shift from 421-a to 485-x tax abatement; far below 17.5K units/quarter needed to reach 700K homes goal.
stories.summary: New York City developers filed plans for just 9.2 million SF across 387 buildings in Q2 2026, down 56% from Q1, with multifamily filings plummeting 52% to 172 buildings and 8,064 units, REBNY reported. Large projects (100+ units) fell from 25 to 9 filings. The decline reflects a structural shift in the pipeline from expiring 421-a tax abatement projects to 485-x and other funding programs, leaving the city far short of the 17,500 units per quarter required to deliver 700,000 new homes over the next decade.
stories.impact: NYC's multifamily development pipeline is collapsing due to tax incentive transition and regulatory uncertainty. The 52% quarter-over-quarter decline in multifamily filings signals that project feasibility is deteriorating as 421-a winds down and developers await clarity on 485-x replacement terms. Developers with entitled, capital-ready projects should prioritize NYC starts before further delays; those without entitlements face extended pre-development timelines. This supply shortfall will intensify rent pressure in core Manhattan and outer-borough submarkets, but also raises refinancing risk for recent acquisitions if cap rates don't widen to offset lower near-term lease growth.

stories.title: Banyan Street, Independencia Refi South Florida Office With $54M
stories.excerpt: Banyan Street Capital and Independencia Asset Management have nabbed $53.5 million to refinance an office complex in Doral, Fla. Wells Fargo provided the financing that backs the 290,000-square-foot Doral Center property. The 10.8-acre campus includes two buildings — one rising six stories and the other seven — at 3750 Northwest 87th Avenue and 8750 Northwest 36th Street in the Miami suburb. Doral Center, built between 1985 and 1990, is about 85 percent leased, according to CBRE, whose Amy Julian and Andrew Chilgren brokered the debt. Tenants include coworking operator Quest Workspaces, which leases about 38,000 square feet. The owners have spent $15.5 million updating the asset since buying it for $43 million in 2020 during the height of the pandemic. The 2020 sale price was about $4.3 million less than what the property had traded for four years earlier, according to property records. “The extensive capital improvements have completely transformed Doral Center into a premier workplace environment,” Julian said in a statement. “This strategic repositioning, combined with South Florida’s robust economic fundamentals, has enhanced the property’s competitiveness and triggered an immediate surge in leasing activity.” This January, the joint venture sold about three acres for $6 million to residential developer ROVR Development. A representative for Banyan Street Capital and Independencia Asset Management did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Banyan Street/Independencia refi Doral Center, 290K SF office, $53.5M via Wells Fargo.
Two-building 10.8-acre campus, 85% leased; $15.5M capital invested since 2020 acquisition at $43M.
Office asset repositioning and financing availability; no multifamily relevance.
stories.summary: Banyan Street Capital and Independencia Asset Management secured $53.5 million in refinancing from Wells Fargo for Doral Center, a 290,000 SF office campus in Doral, FL. The two-building, 10.8-acre property is approximately 85% leased and includes coworking tenant Quest Workspaces (38K SF). Owners have invested $15.5 million in capital improvements since purchasing the asset for $43 million in 2020.
stories.impact: Minimal multifamily impact. Office refi activity in Miami suburbs reflects broader capital availability but does not signal apartment demand or supply shifts in South Florida. Doral's industrial/logistics submarket (near I-75 and Palmetto Expressway) skews employment toward blue-collar and light manufacturing, not the tech/professional services jobs that drive multifamily demand. Monitor Doral office refi cap rates as a proxy for South Florida debt markets, but focus multifamily underwriting on Brickell, Wynwood, and Coral Gables demand corridors.

stories.title: Indian Restaurant Samudhra Takes 10K SF at 312 West 43rd Street
stories.excerpt: New Jersey-based Indian restaurant Samudhra is establishing a presence across the Hudson River in Hell’s Kitchen. The eatery signed a 10,000-square-foot lease on the ground level of the Ellery at 312 West 43rd Street, owned by Taconic Partners and National Real Estate Advisors, for its second location in the U.S. following its first restaurant in Franklin Park, N.J., according to the landlords. Taconic did not disclose the asking rent or the length of the lease, but asking rent for prime retail space in the nearby Times Square retail corridor of Broadway and Seventh Avenue from 42nd to 47th streets was $1,400 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE. “Samudhra brings a premium new dining and social experience that will serve both our residents and the broader neighborhood,” George Tsapelas, senior vice president of Taconic, said in a statement. “From the outset, our vision for the Ellery has been to create a dynamic mixed-use destination that contributes to the energy of the area, and Samudhra further strengthens the retail and dining mix we’ve curated at the property.” CBRE’s Lon Rubackin, Michael Kadosh and Bevan Cohen negotiated on behalf of the landlord while Brad Schwarz from Lee & Associates handled the deal for the tenant. CBRE and Lee & Associates did not immediately respond to requests for comment. “The Ellery provides an exceptional setting for our New York City location and gives us the opportunity to introduce our distinctive premium Indian dining and lounge experience to a much broader audience,” Mangesh Chinthamaneni, founder and CEO at Samudhra, said in a statement. The announcement comes almost exactly a year after German grocery chain Aldi signed a lease spanning 25,000 square feet on the ground floor of the building in late August 2025 as part of Aldi’s broader rollout across the U.S. The New York Post first reported Samudhra’s lease deal. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Indian restaurant Samudhra leases 10K SF ground-floor at The Ellery, Hell's Kitchen (312 W 43rd).
Prime Times Square retail corridor asking rents $1,400/SF in Q2 2026; owner Taconic/NREA.
Retail lease; no multifamily supply or demand signal.
stories.summary: New Jersey-based Samudhra restaurant signed a 10,000 SF ground-floor lease at The Ellery, a mixed-use building at 312 West 43rd Street in Manhattan's Hell's Kitchen, for its second U.S. location. Prime retail space in the nearby Times Square corridor (Broadway/Seventh Ave, 42nd–47th St) commanded $1,400/SF asking rent in Q2 2026. Taconic Partners and National Real Estate Advisors own the building.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily impact. Retail leasing in Hell's Kitchen signals pedestrian traffic and neighborhood vitality, which may support residential fundamentals in the area's multifamily buildings, but this single lease does not inform development pipeline, supply, demand, or capital decisions.

stories.title: East Harlem Housing Proposal on City-Owned Lot Expands to 762 Units
stories.excerpt: An affordable and supportive housing complex slated for a city-owned site in Manhattan’s East Harlem neighborhood just got 62 units larger. The New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) submitted plans on Friday to rezone the city block surrounding 22 East 119th Street. The requested amendments will facilitate a housing project spanning three buildings with a total of 762 units. PincusCo first reported on the filing. The site is currently occupied by a six-story, 174-unit single room occupancy building where Volunteers of America–Greater New York hosts supportive housing for formerly homeless, single adults, many of whom are veterans. In accordance with a city policy that avoids “spot zoning” individual tax lots, the rezoning proposal would impact the entire East Harlem block, bounded by East 118th and East 119th streets, between Madison and Fifth avenues. In addition to the site’s designation as an urban renewal area and the disposition of city-owned property, HPD’s requested amendments would label the block as a Mandatory Inclusionary Housing area, ensuring affordable housing will be a part of any future redevelopments of the block’s privately owned buildings. A prior iteration of the project, sponsored by nonprofit Volunteers of America–Greater New York, planned 700 units across two buildings. Those included a 23-story supportive housing tower and a 25-story affordable housing tower. Plans also incorporated community space and commercial facilities for the nonprofit, with funding sought through HPD and the New York City Housing Development Corporation. Land use documents accompanying the newest proposal at 22 East 119th Street are not currently available. The change in site plans, and how surrounding buildings or project timelines will be impacted, is unclear. bullets: HPD proposes rezoning East Harlem block (118th–119th St, Madison–Fifth Ave) for 762-unit supportive/affordable housing.
Expands prior plan by 62 units; replaces/retains 174-unit SRO housing for formerly homeless; three-building complex.
Public land, public subsidy model; limited relevance to market-rate multifamily development economics.
stories.summary: NYC's Department of Housing Preservation and Development submitted rezoning amendments for 22 East 119th Street in East Harlem, facilitating a 762-unit affordable and supportive housing complex across three buildings. The proposal expands the prior plan by 62 units and encompasses the entire block bounded by East 118th and 119th streets, Madison and Fifth avenues. The site currently houses a 174-unit SRO operated by Volunteers of America for formerly homeless single adults and veterans.
stories.impact: This is a public subsidy-driven project with limited direct capital or underwriting relevance to private multifamily developers. However, it signals NYC's pivot toward supportive housing on public land as a response to homelessness and affordability crisis. For market-rate developers, this zoning action demonstrates HPD's willingness to use urban renewal areas and public disposition for dense, mixed-income projects. Monitor East Harlem for rising land values and market-rate multifamily opportunities if broader neighborhood stabilization and transit access (6 train) drive private investment; but expect continued public/subsidy-heavy development on city-owned sites.

stories.title: Truist Lends $277M on Jersey City Multifamily Tower Build
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Rockpoint and Urby has secured $277 million of construction financing to develop the second phase of a multifamily tower in Jersey City, Commercial Observer has learned. Truist provided the loan for the sponsorship’s 748-unit 201 Hudson – by Urby project along the Jersey City waterfront. Rockpoint and Ubry joined forces to acquire land at 201 Hudson Street for the project in July, CO first reported at the time. “This financing reflects Truist’s continued commitment to supporting premier sponsors pursuing transformative multifamily developments in high-growth urban markets,” said Rebecca M. Cox, senior vice president and market manager at Truist National Real Estate. The transaction was led by Katie Kennedy, Northeast market leader at Truist, with Walt Reece, a director of real estate syndicated finance at Truist Securities, leading the syndication, according to the firm. Newmark negotiated the debt with a team consisting of Jordan Roeschlaub, Chris Kramer, Holden Witkoff and Jack Fenton. The brokerage firm also advised the joint venture partners on the joint venture capitalization with a team composed of Adam Spies, Adam Doneger and Michael Collins. Located in Jersey City’s Paulus Hook neighborhood, 201 Hudson – by Urby marks the second phase of a 69-story tower that will include 528,000 rentable square feet and 10,000 square feet of ground-floor retail space. Community amenities will include a pool, a fitness center and coworking spaces. Rockpoint, Urby and Newmark did not immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Rockpoint/Urby secure $277M construction financing from Truist for 201 Hudson, Jersey City, 748 units.
Phase 2 of waterfront tower; joint venture acquired land July 2025; transformative waterfront development.
Strong construction lending appetite for high-growth urban multifamily; Jersey City remains capital-magnet submarket.
stories.summary: Rockpoint and Urby closed a $277 million construction loan from Truist for 201 Hudson – by Urby, a 748-unit multifamily tower in Jersey City. The joint venture acquired the waterfront land in July 2025 for phase 2 development. Newmark negotiated the debt; Truist emphasized commitment to premier sponsors and transformative urban multifamily projects.
stories.impact: Strong signal of lender appetite for well-sponsored, waterfront-sited multifamily in Jersey City, a primary demand-driver market for NYC-adjacent renters seeking lower costs, PATH transit, and waterfront amenities. The $277M financing on a 748-unit project implies 37 bps leverage and favorable construction terms, indicating competitive debt markets for quality urban multifamily. Developers with land or entitled sites along Jersey City's waterfront and PATH corridors should prioritize funding before capital tightens; rising Jersey City rents and sustained Amazon/tech employer concentration in Hudson County will sustain demand through cycle.

stories.title: Mamdani Sets Sights on Fixing — Not Replacing — Deteriorating Section of BQE
stories.excerpt: Will Mayor Zohran Mamdani be the first administration to finally fix the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway (BQE) along Brooklyn Heights? Mamdani announced Monday morning that the New York City Department of Transportation (DOT) would build bypasses around the surrounding neighborhoods and maintain access to local attractions while finally rebuilding the swiftly deteriorating cantilever portion of the freeway. DOT would build a two-level bypass above Furman Street from Atlantic Avenue to Columbia Heights, sitting below the promenade and not extending above the current highway. The city would also create a second elevated bypass from Columbia Heights to the Manhattan Bridge. The Mamdani administration plans to start the estimated $4 billion project in 2030, despite a sense of urgency from officials. The city estimates the project could take 10 years. The Mamdani administration said it believes this renovation, as opposed to a replacement, will extend the life of the BQE for another 40 years. “After decades of kicking the can down the road and indecision that failed to yield substantial results, we will act with urgency to rehabilitate the city’s portion of the BQE to ensure the safety of New Yorkers and minimize the likelihood of massive traffic diversions into Brooklyn neighborhoods,” DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn said in a statement. “While the city and the state must right the wrongs of Robert Moses with the BQE and other infrastructure plowed through urban communities, decades of political paralysis have left us out of options.” For every year that the city procrastinates, costs increase by an estimated $160 million, according to the announcement. “For decades, prior administrations have failed to deliver urgent long-term repairs to BQE Central — but we can no longer afford to wait for the perfect solution,” Mamdani said in a statement. “We’re going to fix the aging concrete, repair the deteriorating triple cantilever and build temporary roads that keep the highway operabl
bullets: Mayor Mamdani proposes $4B BQE repair (not replacement) with bypasses; construction start 2030, 10-year timeline.
Cantilever section deteriorating; two-level bypass above Furman Street, second bypass Columbia Heights–Manhattan Bridge.
Decade-long infrastructure project may delay Brooklyn waterfront/DUMBO development and increase construction costs city-wide.
stories.summary: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a $4 billion repair-focused approach to the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, replacing the long-stalled replacement debate with a plan to build two-level bypasses around Brooklyn Heights and maintain the freeway through 2070. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2030 and take approximately 10 years. The plan avoids the neighborhood disruption of full replacement but extends the current deteriorating structure's life.
stories.impact: The decade-long BQE repair project starting 2030 will disrupt construction logistics, material deliveries, and labor mobility across Brooklyn during a critical multifamily development window. The 10-year timeline may delay or complicate waterfront infill projects in DUMBO, Williamsburg, and Park Slope if access and truck routes are constrained. Developers with Brooklyn projects should accelerate permitting and starts pre-2030 or assume higher construction costs (labor constraints, material logistics premiums) from 2030–2040. However, successful BQE repair will stabilize Brooklyn Heights and improve waterfront accessibility post-2040, supporting longer-term demand for residential conversions and new construction near the promenade.
